summary:
Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory of the United Kingdom in which local legislation governs; United Kingdom statutes do not extend automatically. Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people. The Human Rights Act has prohibited discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation since 2013, when the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which also banned age discrimination; gender identity is not a protected ground, so trans people have no statutory protection against discrimination. Proposals to extend that protection were failed or dropped in 2004–2006 and again in 2009.

The sources identify no Bermuda-specific provisions on identity documents or gender markers, border or airport screening, restroom and facility access, custody, healthcare, penalties or protection machinery for transgender people. The absence of gender identity as a protected ground is the only trans-specific legal finding the record carries.

The record describes expression of gender identity as often difficult and documents one instance of official interference: in 2006 the Government attempted to bar Mark Anderson, the drag performer known as the "Queen of Bermuda" Sybil, from participating in a parade, stating that he contradicted local mores and sensitivities. The most recent documented instance of this kind in the record is from 2006; no later instance is documented.

Same-sex marriage has been unavailable since 2022. The Supreme Court legalised it in May 2017 in the Godwin and DeRoche case; the Domestic Partnership Act 2017, given royal assent 7 February 2018 and effective 1 June 2018, replaced marriage with domestic partnerships for both same-sex and heterosexual couples, making Bermuda the first jurisdiction to revoke marriage equality. The Supreme Court restored marriage on 6 June 2018 and the Court of Appeal on 23 November 2018, but the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council banned it again on 14 March 2022, with July 2022 laws retrospectively backdating prior legality. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship should expect no marital recognition.

Consensual sex between adult men was decriminalised in 1994 when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to remove two Criminal Code sections, replacing prior liability of up to ten years' imprisonment for anal and oral sex; lesbian activity was never illegal. As of 2022 the age of consent stands unequal at 18 for consensual anal intercourse under the law effective 1 November 2019 against 16 for other sexual activity, and the gross indecency provision between men was repealed in 2019.

Organised religious hostility toward visible same-sex couples is documented: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (the Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, 12 July) as "incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre". Such hostility is aimed at couples read locally as same-sex, which would reach a trans visitor whose relationship is read that way.
tangentialFactors:
The 1994 decriminalisation debate split the island: religious leaders were divided and the Christian Coalition staged marches against the change, evidence of an organised constituency for the conduct-based restrictions that remained in the Criminal Code.

In November 2020 reporting, the Government spent approximately £150,000 to appeal an unconstitutional case against a man charged and threatened with jail under the "obscene behaviour law" for importing DVDs of gay porn into Bermuda, an expenditure of public funds defending a prosecution of same-sex material.

A prior higher age of consent of 18 for gay male conduct was found in violation of the European Convention on Human Rights, which produced the equalised-but-still-split consent structure in force from 1 November 2019: 18 for anal intercourse, 16 for other sexual activity.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples may adopt equally under the Adoption of Children Act following the February 2015 Supreme Court ruling on marital-status and sexual-orientation discrimination, and the Supreme Court granted binational same-sex partners equal employment and benefits in November 2015.

The Bermuda Regiment, formed by random lottery-style conscription, officially prohibits discrimination or harassment of LGBT soldiers and does not discriminate on grounds of sexual orientation, though such conduct has been reported as tolerated by officers to the extent that one conscript described the Regiment as "the most homophobic environment that exists".

Gay and bisexual men may donate blood with the Bermuda Hospitals Board if they have not had sex with another man in the past 12 months, with a 12-month deferral likewise applied to women who have sexual relations with men who have sex with men.

Protection on the ground of sexual orientation arrived only after failed and dropped proposals in 2004–2006 and 2009; gender identity was not added at any point in that sequence.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether local authorities recognise a changed gender marker on a foreign passport or identity document is not sourced; the record contains no provision either way, and this remains unresolved rather than permissive or restrictive.

The record contains no trans-specific violence or homicide figures for Bermuda, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be made, and no incident involving a transgender person after the 2006 parade episode is documented. An undocumented present is not evidence of an absent risk.

The year of the Norwegian Dawn cruise protest is not given in the source, which dates it only to 12 July; the year remains unresolved.

Whether the Human Rights Act's sexual-orientation protection has ever been applied to conduct or presentation read as gender-nonconforming is not sourced, and no reported enforcement or complaint machinery specific to transgender people is identified.
